title: Ashoka and his edicts: what the inscriptions say
seo_title: Ashoka and His Edicts: Rock Edicts, Pillars and Dhamma
meta_description: Ashoka and his edicts explained: major and minor rock edicts, pillar edicts, where they are found, the Brahmi script, Kalinga and what Ashoka meant by dhamma.
summary: Ashoka (Aśoka), the third Mauryan emperor, ruled about 268 to 232 BCE. He had his messages carved on rocks and pillars across the subcontinent, mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script. These edicts describe his remorse after the Kalinga war and his policy of dhamma: ethical conduct, tolerance and public welfare.

paras: Ashoka was the son of Bindusara and grandson of Chandragupta Maurya. Buddhist chronicles say he served as governor at Ujjayini and Taxila and came to the throne after a struggle among the princes. Those chronicles, written centuries later, also tell dramatic stories of his early cruelty that historians treat with caution.

In his own inscriptions he calls himself Devanampiya Piyadasi, beloved of the gods, of gracious look. The name Ashoka appears in only a few of them, the first found being the Maski minor rock edict in Karnataka, discovered in 1915. That find confirmed that Piyadasi of the edicts and Ashoka of the Buddhist texts were the same person.

sections.h2: The Kalinga war and Rock Edict 13
paras: In about the eighth year of his reign Ashoka conquered Kalinga, roughly present-day coastal Odisha. Rock Edict 13 records that a hundred and fifty thousand people were deported, a hundred thousand killed and many more died. Ashoka says he felt deep remorse and that conquest by dhamma was now the only conquest he valued.

The edict is unusual among royal inscriptions anywhere for expressing regret. Interestingly, Rock Edict 13 is missing from the versions at Dhauli and Jaugada, which stand in Kalinga itself. There, separate edicts addressed to local officials appear instead, urging fair treatment of the people.

Scholars group the inscriptions by form and content. Most are in Prakrit written in Brahmi. In the north-west, at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra, the script is Kharosthi, and at Kandahar in Afghanistan there are Greek and Aramaic versions. James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837 largely using these inscriptions; our guide to the [Brahmi script](brahmi-script.html) tells that story.

sections.h2: What did Ashoka mean by dhamma?
paras: Ashoka's dhamma (Sanskrit dharma) was not simply Buddhism. The edicts set out a general code of conduct meant for everyone in the empire, whatever their sect. Its main points appear again and again.
list: Respect for parents, elders and teachers, and kindness to servants and slaves.
Generosity to Brahmins and shramanas (renunciants) alike.
Restraint in speech, and honouring other sects as well as one's own (Rock Edict 12).
Limits on killing animals, including in the royal kitchen (Rock Edict 1).
Public works: wells, shade trees, rest houses, and medical care for people and animals (Rock Edict 2).
Officials called dhamma-mahamattas to spread these ideas and hear complaints.

sections.h2: How to read an Ashokan edict on site
paras: Most edicts are cut into natural boulders, so they can be hard to spot at first. Look for neat horizontal lines of small, geometric letters: circles, crosses and right angles that are typical of Brahmi. Pillars carry the text in a band at about eye level or above. Many sites have an ASI board with a translation, and these are worth reading before you look at the stone.

A short [Brahmi workshop](write-like-asoka-s-scribes-a-brahmi-workshop.html) is enough to recognise common words like dhamma and devanampiya. Our guide to [what epigraphy is](what-is-epigraphy.html) explains how scholars read and date inscriptions more generally.

sections.h2: What the edicts tell historians beyond dhamma
paras: Read closely, the edicts are also administrative documents. They name officials such as rajukas, pradeshikas and yuktas, mention inspection tours every five years, and refer to provincial centres at Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri. Their find-spots, from Kandahar to Karnataka, map the reach of Mauryan power.

Rock Edict 13 names five contemporary Hellenistic kings, including Antiochus II of Syria and Ptolemy II of Egypt. Because their reigns are known from Greek sources, these names help fix Ashoka's dates. The edicts also show Ashoka's limits: he warns the forest peoples that he has power as well as compassion, a reminder that dhamma was backed by a state.

sections.h2: Ashokan edicts and pillars in Delhi
paras: Delhi has three Ashokan objects. The minor rock edict at Srinivaspuri, near East of Kailash, was found in 1966 and is still in place on its boulder. The Delhi-Topra pillar, carrying all seven pillar edicts, was moved from Topra in Haryana by Firoz Shah Tughlaq in the 14th century and set on top of his palace at [Firoz Shah Kotla](firoz-shah-kotla.html). The Delhi-Meerut pillar stands on the Ridge near Hindu Rao Hospital.

For the full Mauryan story, read our guide to the [Mauryan empire](mauryan-empire.html). The pillar and stupa at Sanchi are covered on our visit to [Sanchi: stupas, gateways and Buddhist art](sanchi-stupas-gateways-and-buddhist-art.html).

faq.q: How many major rock edicts did Ashoka issue?
faq.a: Ashoka issued fourteen major rock edicts, found together as a set at several sites including Girnar in Gujarat, Kalsi in Uttarakhand, Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra in Pakistan, and Erragudi in Andhra Pradesh. Dhauli and Jaugada in Odisha have most of them plus two separate Kalinga edicts.

faq.q: In which language and script are Ashoka's edicts written?
faq.a: Most are in Prakrit, a group of early Indian languages, written in the Brahmi script. In the north-west some are in Kharosthi script, and at Kandahar in Afghanistan there are Greek and Aramaic versions.

faq.q: Which edict mentions the Kalinga war?
faq.a: Major Rock Edict 13 describes the Kalinga war, the deaths and deportations it caused, and Ashoka's remorse. It also names Greek kings of the time, including Antiochus II, which helps historians date Ashoka's reign.

faq.q: Which edict first mentioned the name Ashoka?
faq.a: The minor rock edict at Maski in Raichur district, Karnataka, discovered in 1915, was the first inscription found that uses the name Ashoka. Most edicts call him Devanampiya Piyadasi. The Gujarra edict in Madhya Pradesh and a few others also name him.

faq.q: Was Ashoka's dhamma the same as Buddhism?
faq.a: Not exactly. Ashoka was a lay Buddhist and some edicts address the Buddhist sangha, but his dhamma, as described in the major edicts, was a general ethical code of tolerance, non-violence, respect and welfare meant for followers of all sects.

posts.hook: The edict about the Kalinga war is missing in Kalinga.
posts.caption: At Dhauli and Jaugada in Odisha, Rock Edict 13, with its regret for the slaughter, was left out. Separate edicts urging officials to treat local people fairly appear instead.

posts.hook: Delhi has an Ashokan edict still on its original rock.
posts.caption: The minor rock edict at Srinivaspuri, near East of Kailash, sits in a small protected enclosure. Go with the ASI translation in hand and look for the neat rows of Brahmi.

posts.hook: Write your name in Ashoka's script.
